1.goal: To say, in one sentence, that the three previous lessons arrive together today.
1.interaction: T–S, one line from you and straight on.
run: Do not explain the route. “Three minutes, and then their questions.”
THIS LESSON CLOSES THE BLOCK. Reread the records of the three previous ones before you start: they are what steers the planning of the next lessons.
1.support: If he asks what is coming, repeat the one line and move.
1.challenge: Ask which of the three previous lessons he expects to need most.
1.monitoring: Whether he starts preparing. The attempt at stage 3 is worth more unprepared.
1.transition: Move on when he is on the next screen.

2.goal: The scene, with the clock in sight.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the brief on screen together.
run: Give him time to read the brief.
Confirm two things: they did NOT come to decide the purchase, and it is three minutes.
Do not anticipate the Q&A questions. The whole lesson depends on him not seeing them.
2.expected: That the meeting decides whether there is a second meeting — not whether they buy.
2.support: If the stakes blur, ask what would have to happen for Diane to book the next call.
2.challenge: Ask which of the three people in the room he is really talking to.
2.monitoring: Whether he treats it as a sales pitch. It is not: they came to decide one thing.
2.evidence: Whether he can say what this meeting decides.
2.transition: Move on when he says what this meeting decides.

3.goal: The three minutes with NO model, no support, no preparation. This attempt is half the evidence of the day.
3.interaction: S speaks for three minutes; you time it and say nothing.
run: Give the instruction below and start.
Call the time out loud only at the end.
DO NOT CORRECT AND DO NOT SUGGEST ANYTHING. Not before, not during.
3.expected: Whatever he has. Very likely: more description than the three minutes hold, and the request arriving late or not at all.
3.support: None here. Anything you add contaminates the baseline.
3.challenge: None here, for the same reason.
3.monitoring: How long he actually took, what he put first, and whether the request appeared at all.
3.evidence: The three numbers — duration, opening, and whether the request came. They are half the evidence of the block.
3.transition: Move on when he finishes — even past three minutes. Going over IS the data.

4.goal: To show what fits in three minutes, AFTER his own attempt.
4.interaction: S classifies alone; T–S on one item only.
run: He classifies the six items.
Discuss only the fourth — what he wants from a minority stake — which almost everyone puts in the wrong place.
exact: Why does that go in the three minutes and not in the answers? (Because it is what THEY said, on their own call, that they came to decide.)
4.expected: Six items sorted, with the minority stake in the three minutes.
4.support: If an item resists, ask whether Diane could book the second meeting without it.
4.challenge: Ask what he would cut if it were ninety seconds instead of three minutes.
4.monitoring: Whether the sorting is by what he wants to say or by what they came for.
4.evidence: How much of his own attempt he himself puts in the wrong column.
4.transition: Move on when the six are classified.

5.goal: For him to find what the three good answers have in common.
5.interaction: S marks on screen, then T–S on the pattern.
run: He marks the three. Then ask what the three he marked start with. (All of them start with the number.)
The call in lesson 2 already said that a no changes price and timeline, not the deal. If he does not remember, remind him — it is the bridge across the whole block.
exact: What do the three you marked start with?
Why is saying four better than saying everyone can? (Because the number is checked in due diligence, and being wrong there costs far more than being small.)
5.expected: The three that keep the conversation, and the pattern named: they open with the number.
5.support: If the pattern will not come, read the three out loud one after another and ask what the first word of each is.
5.challenge: Ask him to answer the same question with a number he would be uncomfortable saying, and to say why it still works.
5.monitoring: Whether he reaches for the comfortable answer over the honest number. That choice is the lesson.
5.evidence: Whether he names the pattern himself.
5.transition: Move on when he names the pattern.

6.goal: The four moves said out loud, one at a time.
6.interaction: T throws the situation; S answers with the move. Four, fast.
run: You throw the situation, he answers with the move. Fast, four times.
Correction here is immediate. After this nothing is corrected until the feedback.
CLOSE THE FOUR MOVES ON THE SCREEN before round one.
6.expected: Four answers, each using one of the moves.
6.support: If a move will not come, give the first three words and let him finish.
6.challenge: Throw a situation where two of the moves would work and ask which he chose, and why.
6.monitoring: Whether the move arrives before the content, or after he has already started answering.
6.evidence: How many of the four come out without the screen.
6.transition: Move on when the four have come out.

7.goal: The production of the block: three minutes and two unseen questions.
7.interaction: Role-play. You are Diane and you do not leave the role.
run: Three minutes of pitch.
Then play the FIRST question — and play it fast, once only. If he does not ask for it back, that is the central finding of the block: note it and move on.
Then the second question, this one at normal speed. It has no technical answer — it is about intent, and it is the only one none of his directors could answer for him.
DO NOT INVITE HIM TO SPEAK. The silence after the question is his to fill.
Record everything.
7.expected: Three minutes with the request inside them, and two answers — the first one asked for again if it was missed.
7.support: If he freezes on the second question, repeat it once, unchanged, and wait.
7.challenge: Add a third question from Mark, on the delivery number, and take the answer in one sentence.
7.monitoring: Whether he asks for the fast question to be repeated, and whether the honest number comes out on the delivery one.
7.evidence: The recording, plus whether he asked for repetition or answered over what he missed. It is the central finding of the block.
7.transition: Move on when both questions have been answered — well or badly.

8.goal: To hand back three points and one number, out loud.
8.interaction: T–S, three points and one measurement.
run: Three points, direct: one that worked, one that did not, and ONE measurement said out loud (the length of the pitch, or the repair count).
If he gave the honest number on the delivery question, say it was the right answer and why — he will remember it in the real meeting.
If he answered over the fast question, show him where. Without softening.
Do not add new content. Round two is the same opening, shorter.
exact: If the number came out honest: “She asked about delivery and you gave her the real number, not the comfortable one. That is what buys the second meeting.”
If he answered over her: “Here. She asked, and you answered over her. Ask for it again: Sorry, could you repeat that?”
8.expected: Three points he recognizes, and one number he had not heard before.
8.support: If he disputes the measurement, play the recording at that point rather than arguing.
8.challenge: Ask him to say, before round two, which of the three he intends to change.
8.monitoring: Whether the point about the fast question lands, or is heard as a detail. It is not a detail.
8.evidence: The three points and the number. They go in the block record.
8.transition: Move on when the three points are on the board.

9.goal: The opening only, in sixty seconds, to someone who has said they are in a hurry.
9.interaction: Role-play, round 2. Only the opening; do not repeat the whole simulation.
run: Sixty seconds, the opening only, to someone who has already said they are short of time.
Do not repeat the whole simulation.
Record this one too. The two recordings from today close the block file.
9.expected: Sixty seconds with the request still in them.
9.support: If he cannot cut, ask what Diane already knows after round one.
9.challenge: Ask for it once more in thirty seconds and see whether the request survives twice.
9.monitoring: What he cuts. If the request goes, what was left is description — and it is the request that makes the next meeting exist.
9.evidence: The second recording, and what he cut. Both close the block file.
9.transition: Move on when the sixty seconds are up.

10.goal: To close the block out loud, and to record the three answers the next planning starts from.
10.interaction: S ticks the list; T–S on the close of the block.
run: He ticks what he recognizes.
CLOSE THE BLOCK WITH HIM, OUT LOUD: four lessons, four recordings, and a baseline that did not exist on Monday. It is exactly what he asked for and never had.
Homework, said out loud and never on screen: the post-class has the three minutes about his real company and the two written answers.
10.expected: Some lines ticked, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If the close feels thin, play ten seconds of the lesson-1 recording next to today's.
10.challenge: Ask when the next meeting in English is, and which of the four moves he takes into it.
10.monitoring: Whether he hears the four recordings as progress or as four attempts. They are the same thing, and only one of the two readings is useful.
10.evidence: BLOCK RECORD, filled before you close: did he ask for repetition or answer over what he missed? in what band does he produce under improvisation, compared with the B1 on file? did he do the four pre-classes? The planning of the next lessons starts from those three answers.
10.transition: Close the lesson, and the block.
